name: E-bike charger wall bracket
notes: Wall-mount bracket that holds our e-bike charger brick (about 600 g) off the garage floor. Drawn for injection molding in glass-filled nylon, with two gussets. Two screws into the wall through the base, two screws into the charger through the upright. First production run is 500 units

analysis.productSummary: A 80 × 60 × 50 mm L-shaped wall bracket with two gussets that holds a 600 g e-bike charger off the garage floor, sold to e-bike OEMs and accessory retailers. At 500 units the molded-nylon plan busts the budget; a bent sheet-metal version hits the same duty for a few dollars a part.
detectedFeatures: Two base through-holes for wall screws
Two upright through-holes for charger screws

materials: Mild steel CRS (1.5 mm, powder coated)
pros: 500 units land near $2,500 total, inside the $4,000 budget
Laser plus brake capacity is idle locally right now
Metal beats nylon for creep under a hot garage load
No mold, so design changes cost nothing
cons: Requires reworking the part as a flat blank with bends
Sharp edges need deburring or a hem
Powder coat or anodize adds a step and 3-5 days

designTweaks.change: Replace the two molded gussets with triangular side flanges bent up from the same blank on 2 mm 5052.
designTweaks.why: Keeps stiffness without welding, and the whole bracket comes off one laser blank and three brake hits.
designTweaks.impact: Removes a weld/assembly operation; roughly 30% lower unit cost.

designTweaks.change: Add 3 mm radius relief notches where the 90° base-to-upright bend meets the side flanges.
designTweaks.why: Stops tearing at the bend intersections on 2 mm aluminum with a 2 mm inside radius.
designTweaks.impact: Eliminates the main scrap driver; near-zero reject rate.

designTweaks.change: Change the four screw holes to 5.5 mm clearance with 82° countersinks, and emboss a 1.5 mm-deep stiffening rib down the upright.
designTweaks.why: Countersinks let flat screws sit flush against the charger; the rib restores the bending stiffness lost going from 3 mm plastic to 2 mm metal.
designTweaks.impact: Doubles upright stiffness at no material cost.

pros: Cheapest part cost once tooling is paid off
Matches the geometry as drawn, gussets included
Fits easily in the idle 400 × 350 × 180 mm presses
cons: Tooling alone exceeds the entire $4,000 budget at 500 units
3 mm nominal wall will sink and warp in glass-filled nylon
GF nylon absorbs moisture and creeps under sustained load

designTweaks.change: Drop nominal wall from 3 mm to 2.3 mm and carry load with 1.4 mm ribs on the base underside and gusset faces.
designTweaks.why: Thinner walls with ribs cut sink marks and cycle time in glass-filled nylon.
designTweaks.impact: ~25% shorter cycle and ~20% less resin per shot.

designTweaks.change: Add 1.5° draft to both gussets and all four 50 mm upright faces, pulling in the base-plate direction.
designTweaks.why: Guarantees a straight-pull, two-plate mold with no side actions or lifters.

designTweaks.change: Open the four screw holes straight along the pull axis with 1 mm counterbores instead of cross-drilled bosses.
designTweaks.why: Cross-axis holes would force a side core and a more expensive tool.
designTweaks.impact: Keeps the tool to two plates; avoids a $1,200 side action.

pros: Prints the drawn geometry, gussets and all, with no tooling
Isotropic nylon strength, easily holds 600 g
Local capacity is idle; first parts in about a week
cons: Only two idle SLS machines with 165 mm build boxes
Part volume of 28 cm³ is the price driver

designTweaks.change: Core out the base plate underside to a 2.5 mm shell, targeting 18-20 cm³ of solid volume.
designTweaks.why: SLS is priced by volume and packing density, not complexity.

designTweaks.change: Orient the bracket 45° nose-up and nest two parts per column in the 165 mm build.
designTweaks.why: Better packing lowers the per-part share of the build cost.
designTweaks.impact: Up to 20% more parts per build.

designTweaks.change: Size the four screw holes 0.3-0.4 mm oversize and add a 0.5 mm chamfer at each entry.
designTweaks.why: Sintered holes shrink and leave a lip that catches screws.

pros: Strongest option; effectively indestructible at 600 g load
Six idle mills locally, no capacity risk
Premium look supports a higher retail price
cons: Cutting 28 cm³ out of a 240 cm³ block wastes 88% of the stock
Two setups unless the design is simplified

designTweaks.change: Start from extruded 6061 angle stock (roughly 75 × 50 × 6 mm leg) instead of solid block, machining only holes and gusset pockets.
designTweaks.why: The L-profile is already there, so you only cut features.
designTweaks.impact: ~50% lower unit cost and one setup removed.

designTweaks.change: Make every internal corner an 8 mm radius so a 12-16 mm end mill can clear the gusset pockets.
designTweaks.why: Large cutters remove material faster and chatter less than small ones.

designTweaks.change: Replace the molded gussets with two 6 mm bolt-on triangular plates laser-cut from the same alloy.
designTweaks.why: Lets the main body finish in one op on a vise stop, with plates nested on an idle laser.
designTweaks.impact: Removes the second setup; about $4 per part.

analysis.topRecommendation: Redesign as a bent 2 mm aluminum 5052 bracket with integral side flanges: about $2,000-3,500 delivered for 500 units, inside budget, in under two weeks on idle local laser and brake capacity. Hold the glass-filled nylon mold until you commit to 3,000-5,000 units, where tooling amortizes below $2 per part.
risks: At 500 units the injection-mold plan costs $5,500-11,000 all-in, well over the stated $4,000 budget.
Glass-filled nylon creeps and softens in a hot garage, so a 600 g load hanging on 3 mm gussets should be tested at 60 °C for 30 days.
The STL shows clearance holes only; wall-anchor type and screw pull-out from drywall versus studs are unspecified and govern real-world safety.
No photos were supplied, so the charger-brick interface fit and cable clearance are unverified against the 80 × 60 × 50 mm envelope.
A uniform 3 mm wall is thick for glass-filled nylon and will sink and warp at the gusset-to-base junctions unless cored.

storyboard.visual: Garage floor: charger brick in a puddle, cord tangled around a bike tire.
storyboard.voiceover: Every e-bike ships with a charger. Nobody ships a place to put it.

storyboard.visual: Hands snap the bracket to the wall, charger clicks into the cradle.
storyboard.voiceover: Two screws to the wall, two to the charger. Thirty seconds.

storyboard.visual: Close-up of the bent flanges as a 600 g weight loads the upright without flexing.
storyboard.voiceover: Formed aluminum. Holds six hundred grams, all day, every day.

storyboard.visual: Laser cutter slicing flat blanks, press brake folding one into finished form.
storyboard.voiceover: One flat blank, three bends. No mold, no six-week wait.

storyboard.visual: Cost card on screen: 500 units, under four thousand dollars, shipped in two weeks.
storyboard.voiceover: Five hundred units, under four thousand dollars, in your warehouse in two weeks.

storyboard.visual: Tidy garage, bike and mounted charger, logo and website card.
storyboard.voiceover: Add it to the box. Your customers will thank you.
